articleTitle: An advanced interface to a switching software version management system
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: For a company to compete successfully in the market for switching systems, it requires a family of high quality products developed at reasonable cost. Since software development accounts for a significant portion of the cost of a switching system, it is imperative that a switching software project use the most productive development environment available. As with all large software projects, version management is a crucial component of this environment. The singular characteristics of the marketplace for switching systems, however, place special requirements on a version management system above and beyond those required for other large software projects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Program structure based on a concurrent object model for switching systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: A switching system program is a large, real-time, long-lived and frequently modified system. The following features are required: good maintainability; rapid introduction of new services; adaptability to enhanced services; and flexibility to increase capacity. A well-structured program is a key factor in meeting these requirements. A new program structure based on the concurrent object oriented model where objects run concurrently, which produces well-structured switching programs is proposed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Systematic high level design of a switching system for stream oriented traffic
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Describes the design of a switching system for stream oriented traffic. The design is obtained through application of a methodology that emphasizes the use of a formal description technique (LOTOS). For this reason, both the implementation independent, highest level description as well as all intermediate designs are expressed in LOTOS. In this way precision is attained where many other methodologies remain vague and ambiguous. Since the design of switching systems presents one of the most challenging tasks in current information technology, the potential benefit for use of a formal and systematic design method is high. The method assists one to fully exploit the parallelism inherently present in the functionality of the system, in the realization of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using PROLOG for rapid prototyping of telecommunication systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Rapid prototyping techniques can be used for the incremental system design of large systems and for the tools required to build them-instead of designing the complete system and then going into a lengthy implementation and test phase, the various components of the system can be prototyped and tested within a very short time. In this manner costly faults in the system design are isolated at an early stage in a project and experiments with alternative implementation techniques can be performed before being committed to a particular technology. The work described in the paper builds upon some of the conclusions of Armstrong et. al. (1986), and in particular addresses the problems of a language for prototyping telephony software. The implementation of a prototyping language, prototyping environment and experiences of using this environment are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software architecture for automated communications software development
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: From a communications software development support viewpoint, various formal description techniques (FDTs) have been studied and proposed. An application method of an FDT based on a concurrent process model that can be fully automatically analyzed is discussed. A target system software architecture that overcomes the lack of FDT expressive power is proposed. The applicability of the method that uses the FDT and architecture, and the performance of the target system are both evaluated through experiments on a key telephone system software development. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves a performance level suitable for practical use and has portability to other target systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SVEX: switching program verification expert system
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The switching program verification expert system (SVEX) automatically detects logical bugs of call handling programs and outputs information for debugging. SVEX can also reverse-engineer the service specifications from the programs. This function is used for detecting service bugs. The functions are implemented by using verification rules and by simulating the actions of programs on an object-oriented switching-system model. SVEX was applied to the development of PBX and detected logical errors automatically, in which the errors overlooked at the functional test using the target switching system were included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software engineering for IBC: towards a reuse-based approach
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The advantages of reuse are particularly relevant to engineering and maintenance of the large volumes of extremely complex software that will be required for Integrated Broadband Communications (IBC). This fact has been recognized in the RACE programme which includes two projects, ARISE and SPECS, that explicitly deal with various aspects of software reuse. ARISE (A Reusability Infrastructure for Software Engineering) (RACE Project 1021) is a five year project whose main concern is to specify the elements of an integrated support environment for the engineering of IBC software. The paper presents the methodological approach adopted by ARISE for achieving results in the area of reuse of relevance to software engineering in the telecommunications domain. It does not say how reuse should be done in the telecommunications domain, but rather describes an approach to applied industrial research on reuse which will yield the results we need.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of SDL to ISDN and OSI
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The complex structure of communication protocols in open communicating systems demands powerful structuring and description tools, especially with the aim of specifying behaviour. The development of the ISDN Protocol Reference Model (ISDN PRM) based on the OSI Basic Reference Model (OSI BRM), the conception of suitable test procedures and the use of formal languages to describe the behaviour of protocols and systems are important factors that influence standardization in this area. However, the development of such tools and aids have proceeded independently, leading to difficulties in integrating them into a single concept. The paper deals with these aspects, particularly in connection with the use of the CCITT's specification language SDL (Specification and Description Language) to model both the architecture and the behaviour of protocols and services within the framework of OSI and the ISDN PRM, the latter especially in connection with the novel ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) concept.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Priority control in software maintenance
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The software maintenance activity on a large, complex program or system is characterised by a large number of requests for action, each of which is given a certain level of priority. The assessment of priority is an important exercise, with impact on the profitability of the system as a whole; yet in practice, subjective methods are the norm. The paper puts forward a scheme for assessing priority on financial grounds, which allows a more objective view to be taken of the situation as a whole.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Protocol testing: using hardware techniques for software
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Describes test and verification tools which make it possible to design and evaluate computer communication software. The tools are based on methods already standard for hardware testing. A short description of the concepts used in hardware testing and communication software (protocol) testing is given. Metrics are introduced to evaluate tests for complicated distributed applications, such as the OSI session layer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ROSA-RACE Open Services Architecture
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The objective of the ROSA project is to develop a model for the RACE Open Services Architecture, and to show its practical relevance to the evolution of software for Integrated Broadband Communications (IBC) during its potential life-span of 25 years or more. Its principal deliverable is the ROSA embryonic standard which will be in the public domain and non-confidential and suitable for input to international standardisation processes. The ROSA project aims to fill a crucial gap in software strategy for the RACE programme by forming a bridge between the Functional Reference Model and the Programming Infrastructure projects. Its definition of a common architectural approach to system engineering design at all levels, which facilitates the evolution of open systems, provides a focus for current Programming Infrastructure projects and an instrument for applying their results coherently and consistently across IBC.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A formal techniques environment for telecommunications software
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The pre-competitive European Community RACE programme is designed to lead to Integrated Broadband Communications (IBC). The paper describes the work of the SPECS (Specification and Programming Environment for Communications Software) project which has the objective to provide maximum automation and optimisation of the whole software process from requirements through specification, design, implementation, test, execution and maintenance. The basis for the methodology is the application of formal methods. The emphasis of the paper is on the methodology and architecture of supporting tools which are under development within the SPECS project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Object support for mobility as a general concept
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: In attempting to discuss the development of telecommunication networks, it will be useful to construct an exemplar which will encapsulate the nature of what is intended. The exemplar will provide information on the technical implementation features which are required for an intelligent network. The properties of the same exemplar will also serve as a user tool, to allow the user to understand what the network has to offer. The users should be able to express their telecomms requirements in terms of the exemplar and thereby effect control over the network according to their service needs. It would be convenient, if the employment of the exemplar by users to formulate their requirements, had a direct correspondence to the use of the exemplar in a subsequent implementation on the network, but this is not essential. The two uses of the exemplar (drawn from object oriented software engineering) are expanded upon.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implementation and evaluation of service process control software for intelligent network services
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Proposes a new hierarchical service control architecture and discusses the implementation of service process control software aimed at achieving service specification independence within an experimental system. The experimental system consists of three subsystems, a network service support point (NSSP), network service control points (NSPs) and service action points (SAPs). The software defined services are mainly provided through the NSSP and NSP software, which are based on compiler/interpreter technologies and a software architecture applied abstract data type (ADT) concept. The NSSP software is the service specification definition software, which contains a service specification language (SSL) compiler. The NSP software is service process control software, which contains an interpreter for service execution instructions and SAP control operations. The SAP has several kinds of network resources, such as audio announcement machines, and audio conference machines. The new hierarchical service control architecture, and the NSP software structure are described and the NSP performance is evaluated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implementing SDL specifications using algebraic reduction techniques
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Proposes a new strategy for automatic code synthesis without the drawbacks of simple translations schemes. Its prime advantage is that the performance of the generated code is insensitive to the way and degree of partitioning of its specifications. By eliminating the 'internal' interprocess communication, it also solves the problem of queue dimensioning. The main idea behind the proposed method is to map SDL onto some kind of process algebra. The problem with SDL is that it is a language and not an algebra: there is no way of telling whether two SDL expressions are equivalent, apart from their being textually identical. Since the semantics of SDL are formally defined (which happened only recently), one can argue that two SDL expressions are equivalent when they exhibit the same behaviour (whatever that may be) but one still lacks operators that can be applied to SDL expressions. By mapping SDL onto a true process algebra, one has the opportunity to apply transformations on a specification, working toward a more efficient implementation while preserving the overall behaviour, and to analyze the specified behaviour.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling security aspects of a Message Handling System in LOTOS
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Describes the formal specification of the security aspects of a Message Handling System (MHS). The authors chose the international standard formal description technique LOTOS to describe this system. The actual system being modelled, called LOCATOR, is a secure mobile MHS, and was developed within the UK's Alvey programme. They outline the MHS, the security services, and describe the modelling of these services in LOTOS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Description of telecommunication systems by means of a functional language
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Shows how a simple functional language can be used for the description of telecommunication systems and complex systems in general. In particular it is shown how such descriptions can be structured to master the combinatorial state space explosion by using features of functional languages like equational function definitions and higher-order functions. The concept of default equations is introduced to support modular decomposition of definitions. There exists a large body of knowledge about formal manipulations of descriptions in functional languages. Some practical applications of this are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: FINE-a feature design environment (for intelligent networks)
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The introduction of intelligent networks will cause a dramatic increase in the number of new features demanded by the telecom market. In order to fulfil these demands, the current software design cycle must be shortened. Simultaneously the software engineering community is trying to handle the software crisis by introducing IPSEs (Integrated Project Support Environments) as the glue for the application tools. FINE (Feature INteractive Environment) is a prototype system, to support the design of feature programs, based on the IPSE architecture. A feature program (e.g. some subscriber service) is implemented as an addition to POTS. The architecture is composed of three main subsystems-UIMS (User Interface Management System), a set of tools and a database.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On SDL-based system design methodology: experience with the SPRITE environment
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Considers the position of SDL in the context of current trends in system development methodology. These considerations and the authors' experience in developing and introducing the specification/design support environment SPRITE are combined to suggest guidelines for further development of both SDL and the environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Engineering embedded knowledge-based software for a digital switching system
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The development of embedded knowledge-based software for digital switching systems and its successful integration to the main stream conventional software demands special approaches not usually emphasised in other environments. Because of the programming-in-the-large and in-the-many characteristics of digital switching systems, disciplined software engineering approach is inevitable. Severe reliability requirements necessitate appropriate support form the programming tools. Cost-effective optimization of hardware resources impose constraints on both application selection and implementation tools. It is shown how a powerful programming environment based on an abstract data types (ADT) language augmented with rule-based facilities can help significantly in meeting the above requirements. The approach is illustrated through XEDA, an embedded knowledge-based application developed at Nokia Telecommunications to improve the diagnostics function of the DX 200 digital switching system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A declarative language for data and telex exchange configuration
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The LEP language is a simple, declarative language designed to define the routing and customizing rules of a telex exchange, but the concepts employed can easily be applied to telephony or data transmission. The language is in accordance with CCITT Series Z.300 Recommendations. The user writes a LEP text using a text editor-possibly in the exchange console-and then follows the normal procedures: compilation, simulation of the configuration programmed, and installation of the latter in the exchange on a resident basis. The compilation programs perform the static error detection tasks and generate the necessary tables. They also supply auxiliary information which help with the simulation and corection of errors involving logical inconsistencies. The paper discusses the general abstraction used in this language based on the present packet switching experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A database model for network services
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: In the United States telecommunications network, network databases are increasingly involved in call processing for the realization of new network services. The authors explore the use of the relational model to describe the application interface to network services data. They illustrate the use of standard relational data manipulation language to express the database interaction logic of several services, including directory services, 800 service, network call distribution and automatic call back. They discuss the advantages of the use of a standard interface between network applications and the data they access and consider the feasibility of implementing the model directly within the network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The automatic deduction of strategies for on-line software extension
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The on-line environment that the IOLE project is to provide implicitly includes the specification of some suitable hardware (HW) architecture. The IOLE project in fact is also to focus current trends in HW design, so as to single out adequate existing processor architectures suitable for Integrated Broadband Communications (IBC), bearing in mind that any future IBCN shall be both multi-country and multi-vendor. The future IBC systems must provide a high degree of flexibility, permitting software changes for the purpose of introducing new services or modifying existing ones. At the same time, IBC systems must offer a high degree of availability. In order to cope with both requirements, on-line software extension mechanisms are needed that offer the possibility to add, delete or replace software within a system without disturbing the activities carrying real traffic. The paper presents initial steps towards a methodology for determining an extension strategy, i.e. a plan for the execution of the extension, to guide the on-line replacement of a particular software component.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The BEST method for requirements capture and functional specification
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: RACE requires a method which allows the formation of consensus between a set of actors, handles the complexity of future telecommunication systems, defines and makes explicit the policies of interested parties. The BEST method is open in the sense that it is not tied to any particular language. It is flexible in the sense that any specification or design language can be used within the framework of the BEST method. The paper describes the BEST method and gives some examples of the types of conceptual models developed using the method. The BEST method supports the requirement definition, specification and design of an abstract system. A key requirement on the method, in order to support the building of consensus, is that all requirements, assumptions, policies and decisions arising during the process are made explicit and open to inspection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ISDN operation and maintenance network architecture
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Introduces a novel operation and maintenance network capable of handling administration tasks pertaining to centralized operation and data management for ISDN exchanges. A particular aspect of the approach is the use of standardized communication protocols based on the OSI remote operation functions and application contexts including application layer protocol conversion facilities (gateways). Three heterogeneous ISDN exchange types in Switzerland (AXE, EWSD, System 12) will be supported. One single protocol type i.e. OSI remote operations covers all communication needs for all systems including bulk data transfer and remote interactive services, this in contrast to the traditional separation of various operation and maintenance protocol types. The protocols and gateways are now fully specified and the implementation of the first application for the billing data collection is in progress. From the beginning on, the underlying bearer network relies on the SWISSNET ISDN circuit switched services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software tools and support environment of the national centre for supervision and management of the Italian telephone network
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The approach followed for the National Supervision Centre (CSN) is based on the principles of object-oriented software design and the finite state model, which allows the construction of systems by composing a set of modules both logically and physically disjointed. Each module can be referred at the same time as an object implementing a set of operations on its encapsulated data or as one of the concurrent communicating processes of the system. The methodology must be supported by a minimum set of procedures for process organisation and message passing. For this, the CCITT specification and description language was selected. After a brief description of the software quality aspects that must be taken into account, the architecture and most significant functionalities of the CSN system are described. Then the methodology is introduced together with examples of application to a real case.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An SDL environment in Occam
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Considers the combination of the CCITT Specification and Description Language (SDL), the Occam programming language, and transputer hardware. The structured use of this combination encourages formality in the total system design process and allows performance to be considered at an early stage in the design. An environment in which an SDL system can be translated to an occam program has been built. The use of this environment assists in producing a correct implementation of SDL, and allows one to estimate the performance of an SDL system on single- and multi-transputer systems at the point of specification.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: HCDM/GSDS-experiences with CASE for telecom systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: CASE (Computer Aided Software Engineering) tools for the software design and implementation phases are intended to shorten the software life cycle and to increase the quality of the resulting products. One way to achieve this goal is to bridge the gap between design and implementation phase by automating the transition from design to code. The paper presents the complete program generation approach of Hierarchical CHILL Design Method/Graphical Software Design System (HCDM/GSDS) and compares it with other approaches. Arguments for the complete generation approach are outlined. Some unsolved technical problems with that approach are discussed based on the practical experience of the application of HCDM/GSDS methods and tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated visual development environment for switching systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: It is important to improve the switching software development environment. The authors analyse the issues and solve them by grasping the switching software development process from the viewpoint of software representation. As shown, representative charts and diagrams that aid in visualization of the software phase from various types of semantics have been developed and applied. These charts and diagrams are called 'views'. Most of these software views have been used to visualize specific processes in the software life cycle, but they are discontinuous. Therefore, the discontinuity of these views hinders the design thought processes (existence of a transformation gap). Further, during verification testing of these processes and functions or performance, the disunion between design and verification hinders the verification processes (existence of an interpretation gap). A view that integrates all processes in the development environment is required. A new visualized environment for software that has overcome the conventional restrictions by using recently developed workstations (WS) is proposed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A specification-based simulation technique for fault recovery process design
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Stored program control switches split their functions between hardware and software; therefore, the effective allocation of functions is important in system design. A fault recovery process simulator is useful in supporting the designer's thinking because he can easily test his ideas for the function allocation and confirm the system behavior with the tool before hardware and software designs become far advanced. The paper describes hardware and software specifications and a simulation technique based on these specifications. The main subjects discussed are: the model of the fault recovery process for hardware faults in ESS; the fault recovery process; user interfaces; and the simulation technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using CORE with SDL to specify requirements
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Describes how the quality of product requirements specifications can be improved through the use of a structured method combined with a well-defined and structured notation. The Controlled Requirements Expression (CORE) method is effective in guiding the analysts through the information capture process; SDL provides a powerful notation for expressing these functional requirements. SDL notation can be used consistently for subsequent design. The contextual modelling approach of CORE enables validation of the specification to be carried out. CORE encourages design constraints to be identified and their effect analysed. The overall match CORE and SDL is extremely good; so good that a hybrid technique which takes advantage of the strengths of CORE and SDL seems a most natural development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An information model for intelligent network services
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Data in the intelligent network will be distributed, and in part replicated, amongst the component nodes of the network; this distributed database provides support for network-wide control and management. The ability to reallocate and restructure the data is essential in order to meet the needs of changing network characteristics and new service functionality. The paper describes a highly structured view of the intelligent network database. The data is classified as a set of entities and relationships between these entities are identified, using the entity-relationship method. The motivation for constructing this model is that it should serve as the basis for methodically producing a clean design of the database. Such a design should be resilient to changes in the physical components, and should also be able to accommodate new service functionality. It will be seen that a single simple model is sufficient to represent both the real-time service information requirements and the service management information requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The feature interaction problem in telecommunications systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The development of telecommunications features is difficult for many of the same reasons that software development is difficult. The need for rapid feature introduction requires separation of applications from the system, allowing multiple vendors to concurrently develop features. A key obstacle to the concurrent development of features, the feature interaction problems is examined. As a framework for studying feature interactions their effects on customers and developers are discussed, and tools and methods that exist or are emerging that reduce their impact on the development process are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic program modification in telecommunications systems
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: In today's public telecommunications network, the logic of telecommunications services is typically defined in software that executes in stored program control switching systems or other network elements. Changes in network functionality require that new versions of software be installed in these network elements, a process that has proven inconvenient and error-prone. The authors expect that changes to network software will occur with increasing frequency in the future, exacerbating the software update problem. They discuss the requirements for performing software updates in the telecommunications network and describe a specific approach that allows dynamic modification of programs running in a distributed environment. They also discuss the implications of this approach for the design of telecommunications software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance analysis in the early design of software
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: Introduces a methodology to transform descriptions of systems into models suitable for performance analysis. The need for metrics and measurements of different system qualities throughout the life-cycle of a system, following the ideas in Rapp and Sjodin (1983) is also discussed. Special emphasis is put on the early design phases in the sense that most of the design-decisions are tried out before implementing the system, to ensure anticipated behaviour. The main idea of the modelling methodology is to divide the system into two model types. One model concerns the use processes of the system, which are reflected in user behaviour and application software. The other model concerns the queue structures and architecture of the system. These two models could be combined in different ways resulting in either a so called Queue-Flow Model or a Performance Prototyping Simulator. The maturity of the models will depend on where in the life-cycle they are developed, i.e. how much information and knowledge are available. The methodology suggested is based on CCITT-SDL for the description of the software. One of its major benefits besides from being a standard is its formal representation, which makes modelling and parameter extraction easier.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: IC*: an environment for designing communications software
publicationTitle: Seventh International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Switching Systems, 1989. SETSS 89.
abstract: The modern phone network offers increasingly sophisticated services provided by increasingly complex software. This software controls and is responsible for maintaining the integrity of many semi-autonomous interacting systems, both hardware and software. Designing, specifying, and implementing such software requires an environment capable of expressing and managing its intrinsic parallelism. The IC* environment is being developed at Bellcore to meet this need. The current environment consists of the L.0 language and supporting tools. L.0 is an inherently parallel, object-oriented language based on the IC* model of synchronous, parallel computation. The current release of L.0 has not been optimized and is being used for simulation and prototyping rather than field release. This release runs on UNIX, IBM MVS, and Unisys 1100 systems and code developed for one is easily ported to the others. Parallel systems are very hard to understand statically, so the heart of the current environment is a set of tools for the audio-visual animation of executing specifications and for the production of prototypes. The designers and implementors of a new software system can observe it in action and play with it. The execution trace of a system's description can also be stored and browsed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
